summary.text: Take \(n=p=2\): the defining products at \(np=4\) both equal \(96\), so \(a(4)=1\) and hence its 2-adic order is \(0\). On the proposed right-hand side, only the \(i=0\) term is nonzero, giving \(\lfloor 2/2\rfloor=1\), so the two sides disagree.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{k=1}^{N}\gcd(j,k)}
{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{N}\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor!\right)^k}.
\]
We disprove the conjecture by taking
\[
n=2,\qquad p=2.
\]
These values satisfy the hypotheses: \(n\) is positive and \(p\) is prime. Since \(np=4\), we first compute \(a(4)\) directly.

For the numerator, the matrix of values \(\gcd(j,k)\), with both \(j\) and \(k\) running from \(1\) to \(4\), is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\gcd(j,k)&k=1&k=2&k=3&k=4\\ \hline
j=1&1&1&1&1\\
j=2&1&2&1&2\\
j=3&1&1&3&1\\
j=4&1&2&1&4
\end{array}
\]
The products of the four rows are respectively
\[
1,\quad 4,\quad 3,\quad 8.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{4}\prod_{k=1}^{4}\gcd(j,k)
=1\cdot4\cdot3\cdot8=96.
\]

For the denominator, consider its four factors separately. They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1:&\quad \left(\left\lfloor\frac41\right\rfloor!\right)^1=(4!)^1=24,\\
k=2:&\quad \left(\left\lfloor\frac42\right\rfloor!\right)^2=(2!)^2=4,\\
k=3:&\quad \left(\left\lfloor\frac43\right\rfloor!\right)^3=(1!)^3=1,\\
k=4:&\quad \left(\left\lfloor\frac44\right\rfloor!\right)^4=(1!)^4=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{4}\left(\left\lfloor\frac4k\right\rfloor!\right)^k
=24\cdot4\cdot1\cdot1=96.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(4)=\frac{96}{96}=1.
\]
Therefore the exponent of \(2\) in the prime factorization of \(a(4)\) is
\[
\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))=\operatorname{ord}_2(1)=0,
\]
since no positive power of \(2\) divides \(1\).

We now evaluate the right-hand side asserted by the conjecture. At \(n=p=2\), it is
\[
\sum_{i\ge 0}
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor 2/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i=0\), since \(2^0=1\), the summand is
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor 2/1\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac22\right\rfloor=1.
\]
For every \(i\ge1\), we have \(2^i\ge2\), and hence
\[
0\le \left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor\le1.
\]
Dividing this integer by \(2\) and taking the floor therefore gives
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor 2/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Thus all terms after the term with \(i=0\) vanish, and the entire sum is
\[
\sum_{i\ge0}
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor 2/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor=1.
\]

The conjectured identity at \((n,p)=(2,2)\) would consequently assert
\[
0=\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))
=
\sum_{i\ge0}
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor 2/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor
=1,
\]
which is impossible. Hence the proposed identity does not hold for every positive integer \(n\) and prime \(p\), so conjecture D is false.
